implementation_notes: scala.concurrent ships a global ExecutionContext backed by a ForkJoinPool whose parallelism defaults to the available processors (scala.concurrent.context.numThreads overrides it); Future { } schedules onto it, so the pool exists without being written. Because it is global and sized to the cores, blocking calls inside a Future starve it unless wrapped in blocking { }, which asks the pool for a compensation thread; the documentation therefore recommends a dedicated ExecutionContext for long-blocking work instead of tuning the shared pool.
code_sketch:
import scala.concurrent.{Future, ExecutionContext}
import scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext.Implicits.global
val one: Future[Result] = Future { load(id) }        // runs on the global pool
val all = Future.traverse(ids)(id => Future(load(id)))
pitfalls: Blocking inside a Future on the global EC can starve the pool; wrap long blocks in blocking { } or use a dedicated EC.
The global pool's parallelism is the core count, not 'unlimited': CPU-bound fan-out beyond it queues behind other work.
An implicit EC imported from the wrong scope silently changes where code runs; pass contexts explicitly when it matters.

variants.name: Dedicated ExecutionContext from a Java Executor
variants.implementation_notes: For a bounded pool with its own policy, wrap a Java executor: ExecutionContext.fromExecutor(new ThreadPoolExecutor(...)) gives Scala futures a private pool with an explicit size, queue and rejection policy - the documented shape for long-blocking work, since it isolates that work from the global EC. This keeps the Java policy surface (bounded queue, handlers, thread factory) while code stays in Future style; shut the executor down explicitly when the component stops.
variants.code_sketch:
val pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
                                  new ArrayBlockingQueue(1_000))
given ec: ExecutionContext = ExecutionContext.fromExecutor(pool)
val f = Future { blockingCall() }                    // isolated from the global pool
pool.shutdown()
pitfalls: ExecutionContext.fromExecutor wrapping a synchronous or single-threaded executor runs futures on the submitting thread, which surprises callers expecting asynchrony.
An EC whose executor was shut down rejects work with RejectedExecutionException, so futures fail instead of running.
Await.result from inside the same dedicated pool deadlocks it; compose with futures or use a second pool for the blocking dependency.
